description: We are Camila (Environmental Geography and GIS) and Federico (Software Development and Remote Sensing). LANDSENSE aims to transform SAR satellite data into accessible information about changes in the Earth's surface, their reliability, and territorial context, supporting risk assessment and decision-making while bringing science closer to the community.
summary: LandSense is an interactive 3D web app that turns real NISAR radar data into plainlanguage stories about how the Earth's surface changed, and how sure we are of each result. NISAR, the NASA–ISRO L-band radar, sees through clouds and at night. We used its interferograms (GUNW) to measure ground motion from earthquakes and its backscatter (GCOV) to map new water from floods. Every finding is checked against a no-event control and an independent source (USGS, NASA OPERA water maps, field surveys) and carries a visible confidence label: verified, validated, indication, or "NISAR cannot measure it". Highlights: about 56 cm of westward ground motion in the June 2026 La Guaira (Venezuela) earthquake, consistent with NASA/JPL, and flood water in Chaco, Argentina, rising from 13% to 87% in the areas NISAR flagged, in a pre-registered blind test. A guided tour in three reading levels (kids, general, in depth) makes radar science accessible to decision makers, teachers and the public. All code is open source.
details: What it does. LandSense tracks two kinds of surface change with NISAR: ground motion from earthquakes and new water from floods. It shows them on a 3D globe with real radar images draped on the terrain, a before/after slider and a timeline of every radar pass. A guided tour plays by itself in three reading levels: kids aged 8–13 (NISAR tells its own story), general public, and in depth with products, dates, methods and sources. An Explore mode lists every M6+ earthquake since June 2026 and floods in Argentina, each with what NISAR measured there, or why it could not. The app is available in English and Spanish. How it works. Open Python scripts read NISAR products by streaming them from NASA Earthdata. For earthquakes, they use GUNW interferograms that span the event, compare them with a pair of dates with no event (control) and combine orbits to separate east–west and vertical motion. For floods, they use GCOV backscatter: the crosspolarized HV echo comes mostly from vegetation and calm water acts as a mirror, so a cell is flagged when its HV echo drops by half or more (−3 dB). Thresholds are fixed beforelooking at the result. Each result is then compared with an independent source (USGS fault models, NASA OPERA DSWx water maps, field surveys by the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team) and labeled: unverified, verified, validated, or retracted. Results shown. La Guaira, Venezuela (M7.5, June 24, 2026): about 56 cm of westward ground motion south of Maiquetía airport, two independent orbits agree (r = 0.98), consistent with NASA/JPL (up to about 60 cm). Coherence loss flags 97 likely-collapse zones that contain 248 of 328 field-verified collapsed buildings. Paraná Delta (August 2026): water in NISAR-flagged areas went from about 5% to about 70% according to NASA OPERA DSWx. Chaco (October 2026, during El Niño): pre-registered blind test, 13% to 87% water in flagged areas versus 7% to 8% in unchanged areas. Panama (M7.7) and Tibet (M7.0) are shown as seen but with their limits stated. Of 41 strong earthquakes, 32 were at sea or too deep: the app says "NISAR cannot measure it" instead of guessing. Benefits and impact. It translates complex radar observations into information that emergency managers, decision makers, teachers and the public can act on: where the ground moved, where to look first for collapsed buildings, which areas flooded under cloud cover, and how much to trust each answer. Showing what radar cannot do is part of the design. Tools. Python 3.11 (numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib, rasterio, pyproj, earthaccess, requests), CesiumJS and Cesium ion terrain, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/fedesina/landsense (Apache 2.0). What comes next. Running the analysis automatically on every new NISAR pass, adding more regions and change types, and other radar missions to fill the gaps between passes.
